speechtext:
I will try and remember to use the adjective in future, but I did not think any man would take exception to my calling him a gentleman. I certainly did not use the' word with any intention of being disrespectful. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Achim), who seconded the motion for the six months' hoist, and who, I believe, also seconded the Address in the session of 1915, spoke as follows on February 8, 1915:
Kot a single one of these men (soldiers) has thought of arguing over his rights or duties not one of them has endeavoured to find out a clause of the Constitution behind which he might find refuge.
Once the enemy is victorious on the continent and is master of the British IsTes, it will he too late to take up arms for the defence of the country.
I suggested a moment ago that defending the Empire under present conditions was equivalent to defending our own country.
I cannot see how the hon. member for Labelle can square his position of to-day

with his utterances in the House which I have just quoted; however, that is up to him.
The case against the referendum could not be better summed up than in the language of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), who said:
The referendum amendment recognizes no need, suggests no remedy, and applies no alternative.
Suppose a referendum is submitted to the people. Who is going to vote on that referendum? All those whose names appear on the voters' lists? If sp, that will include thousands of Austrians and Germans who have been in this country perhaps only four or five years, and who might reasonably be expected to still have a warm regard for Austria and Germany. Would it be fair to all.ow these men to poll their votes on the referendum, when it would .be impracticable to obtain the votes of the soldiers in the trenches? There is also in this country a certain sect called Mennon-ites, who I understand settled here on the distinct pledge of the Government that they would not be called on for military service. Their names, however, appear on the voters' lists. Would it be fair to allow these men who are exempt .from military service to cast their vote in the referendum, when the soldiers at the front would not be allowed to cast theirs? I think it is only necessary to state these obvious objections to convince any person that this referendum should not receive the consideration of any person in this House or in the country. We are told that if the referendum carried it would be put into effect. What warrant have we for thinking that? Some yeats ago the right hon. gentleman who to-day leads the Opposition gave a distinct pledge to the people of 'Canada, when leader of a great party in this country, that if returned to power he would submit the question of prohibition to the people by way of referendum, and if the majority of the people of Canada decided in favour of prohibition, prohibition they should have. As it happened, the majority of the people of Canada did decide in favour of prohibition, but the majority of the people of the province of Quebec voted against prohibition, and the right hon. gentleman did not attempt to carry out his pledge to give the people of Canada a prohibition law.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) in his address the other evening said that the British-born in this coun-. try are against the Bill, that they had left the country so as not to be called upon for

military service. I take strong exception to that. The manner in which the British-born have answered the call does not warrant the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe in making any such insinuations as that. His remarks were entirely unfair, uncalled for, and quite incorrect. He also took exception to the statement of the Solicitor General that the Bill in its working out would bear more lightly on the province of Quebec than on other provinces for reasons which the Solicitor General gave. Commenting on this, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Air. Gauthier) said:
We resent the insult whether direct or indirect. Thank Heaven we do not belong to a race of cowards. We are willing to do our share to the bitter end, and no man in this House nor in this country can tell us that if we vote for the Bill we shall be exempted. We do not want to be put in reserve.
It is quite proper to mention that supporting this motion for a referendum is doing that very thing. The sentiment of the province of Quebec is undoubtedly against conscription, if we are to 'believe what we read in the press and what is stated in this House by some hon. members. I contend that the course taken by the leader of the Opposition has the effect of placing the province of Quebec in reserve. I also wish to call attention to the closing words of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe :
I say to the "Government:	If you press
this measure through, my people, declaring that this Government has no mandate, will use the very Bill itself to fight the matter out. We acknowledge that in this fight there will be pain and suffering. We may have to go to the direst consequences. My people are willing to go to the limit if you impose upon them such a piece of legislation; I believe they are right, and I will do as they intend to do.
That language is not calculated to bring recruits from the province of Quebec, nor to bring unity in this country. It is most unfortunate language for any hon. member of this House to use. Are we to believe that if this Bill passes-and becomes law- and it can only pass by obtaining the support of a majority of the representatives of the people gathered here from all parts of Canada-that the people of the province of Quebec will resist it to the point of violence? That is the only inference we can draw from the statement made by the hon. gentleman. If I were to make a statement of that kind in this House hon. gentlemen from Quebec would resent it very strongly, and would say that I had no right to dse such language. I say that we have as much right to resent such a statement coming from one of the members from the

province of Quebec as they would have to resent such a statement if made by myself. If the hon. gentleman's statement is true] we are certainly face to face with a most serious condition. The people of this country, no matter of what nationality, must understand that when the representatives of the people pass a law that law is to be obeyed. We cannot take any other ground. We cannot overlook the fact that we have people here drawn from all parts of the globe, people of all nationalities; and if the people of any one nationality carry resistance against the law to the point of violence, they are simply giving encouragement to those of other nationalities who know less about our laws and institutions, to do likewise. It is a state of affairs that cannot be tolerated for one moment.
The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) said that there was no call from the men overseas to come to their help. I may again refer him to the words of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) to which I referred at the beginning of my remarks. We have a call from the men overseas, from the very soldiers who are on the battle line. We have a call from a Canadian leader, General Currie, who is in command of our men overseas. We have a call from the men who have fallen. We have a call from those who have been in the trenches doing their bit for 'months and months.
Some hon. gentlemen have advised the Government to postpone the bringing into effect of this Act. I do not agree with that view, and I will give my reasons. There are hundreds of men overseas to-day who never should have left Canada; there are hundreds and thousands of men in Canada who should be overseas. The voluntary system was all right, up to a time. By that system we were gathering men faster than we could equip them and send them overseas. But every hon. member knows that there came a time when it seemed necessary to send men out on the platform to urge, and, it would seem, to cajole and browbeat men into joining the ranks. There are some men who had courage enough to face the German bullets who had not courage enough to face the reputation of being slackers. As a result, many of these men who had not the courage to face the sneers of their compatriots enlisted and went overseas though they should never have gone. During the last week I received a letter from a lady in my constituency asking me to intercede with the Government to have her son returned. He is her only son. Her
husband is ill and has been sent to a hospital, and will not be able to take up farm work. So that lady and her daughter are left to run a farm of 125 acres with about 25 head of cattle. That young man ought never to have gone overseas. But there are others who could be spared, easily spared, and who should be over there to take his place.
Furthermore, I wish to impress upon the House, in all fairness to the boys at the front, one plain fact. Many of those men have been over there a year and a half or two years, or more. They have been called upon to endure extreme hardship in the trenches. These men have bravely offered themselves and are ready to face all dangers. Under present conditions, they are kept on the firing line week after week and month after month, without any chance to rest and recuperate. These men are not only doing their bit but each of them is doing the bit of two or three others who are staying in Canada and making big money. That is not fair, it is not just, it is not right, it is not reasonable. I appeal to hon. members of this House to give this matter their earnest and careful and favourable consideration. I urge them to support this Bill, for I am firmly convinced that it is the only way in which we can at the present time supply the reinforcements for our men at the front of which they stand so much in need. We are not worthy the sacrifices they have made if we do not give them the reserves they need and the support they expect at our hands.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject which is now before the House for discussion is certainly one of the most serious subjects we have had to decide on since Confederation, and no doubt one of the most serious subjects since the time of the cession of this country fr am the French to the English. In the few remarks which I purpose making this evening, I am going, even at the risk of lese majeste, to treat the subject purely and simply from the point of view of a Canadian. I might preface what I intend to say by a word or two in answer to the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Edwards). He asks the question, why is it * that in the province of Quebec there should not be more enthusiasm in favour of eon-



scription. If I know anything about the province of Quebec, and I think I do, I have no hesitation in telling him that speeches such as be delivered this afternoon, and such as were delivered by the hon, member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) yesterday, have more to do with inciting the people of Quebec against conscription than anything else I know of. When an hon. member of this House stands up to give his views upon a certain subject, and a subject of the gravity of the present one, and contents himself solely with making an attack upon one province, and then asks that province to be enthusiastic towards the measure which he pretends to advocate, I desire to say that such a position is illogical. I wondered when I heard those attacks whether those hon. gentlemen really wished to win this war or really wished to damn the province of Quebec. The hon. member from Frontenac has asked two questions. One is:	Where was my right hon. friend
the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in connection with the Boer war? The next question was : What was his position in the Imperial Conference, or Conferences? Whilst I am speaking I propose to say a few words as to the position of the leader of the Opposition both in connection with the Boer War and in connection with the Imperial Conferences. Further than that, the hon. member for Frontenac will pardon me if I pass over his other remarks in silence, as I think this House would have been better off, certainly Canada would have been better off, and certainly national unity would have been better off, if such utterances as he made had never been made in this House or out of it.
Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the measure which is before the House until it is submitted to the people for their opinion. Personally, I stand with the great majority of the people of the province of Quebec upon that ground and, personally again, when I say that I'am opposed in principle to conscription, with the people of Quebec I am ready to forego my personal opinion and submit to the popular will. I am opposed personally to the measure before the House, first, because I do not believe that it is, in its present form, constitutional. Even if it were constitutional, it would so affect the national life of this country as to constitute a radical * change which neither you, Sir, nor myself, nor, I claim, any hon. member of this House with the powers and the mandate which we have held since we were elected,
has a righit to commit the people to without their having first had an opportunity of pronouncing upon it. I say I do not believe that the measure in its present form is constitutional. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) has made the statement in this House that the principle of conscription for overseas service has been in the law since the time of the Act which was passed by Sir George Etienne Cartier and the members of /this House in 1868. I want to deal with that question for a very few minutes. The section referred to is section 69 of the Militia Act, reading as follows:
The Governor in Council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
When Sir GeoTge Etienne Cartier introduced that Act, he spoke as follows in this House on the 17th February, 1868:
I deny that the proposed military system of the late Government would have implied, as Mr. Rankin asserted, the putting in usage of conscription.
" Pour mettire en usage la conscription " are the exact French words. Again, on the 31st March 1868, he said:
The sole essential difference between this Bill and the one we proposed in 1862 is upon the subject of enrolment for which I did not ask consent. Under this new law enrolment by captains will cost $32,000.
Throughout all the speeches, if you read them carefully, you will find the idea of providing for military defence is based upon possible incursions or invasions from the United States. So strong was that idea in the minds of the legislators of that day, and immediately prior to it, that we find that Lord Carnarvon, in introducing the British North America Act in the British House of Commons, after bis conference with the delegates of the Dominion of Canada, used this language:
The question of military defence is a somewhat delicate one on which to touch. Military defence supposes war, and war in that part of the world could only be with that great Republic which lies south of our border.
Not only was that the doctrine followed by the men of 1867 and 1868 but, Sir Adolphe Caron, later on Minister of Militia and Defence, in introducing into Parliament the Act of 1883, which was practically a reproduction of the Act of 1868, spoke as follows in the House as reported in Hansard of April 10, 1883:

In Sir George Cartier's time, as now fortunately, we did not require a force for any aggressive purpose, or any other purpose, save securing ' the safety of the person, protecting property, and defending ourselves against any attack which might, as previously, give us occasion to resist and repel any disorganized, or small organized band crossing the frontier.
That position was thoroughly well recognized by the Prime Minister, because in the message which was sent by His Royal Highness the Governor General on August 1, 1914, we find:-
A question has been mooted respecting the status of any Canadian force serving abroad, as' under section 69 of the Canadian Militia Act, the active militia can only be placed on actual service beyond Canada for the defence thereof.
At that time there was just as much necessity of placing the militia of Canada beyond Canada overseas as there is to-day; but the Prime Minister did not wish to take that attitude in this House and commit himself as a constitutional lawyer without saying that he had very grave doubts in his mind as to whether he could rightly take that attitude, and he sought the advice of the Imperial authorities.
The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) wished to know what was the attitude of the right hon. leader of the Opposition at the Imperial Conferences. I will tell him that at the Conference of 1902 a memorandum of the War Office contained the .following:-
Prior to the outbreak of the war in South Africa, so far as any general scheme for the defence of the Empire as a whole had been considered, it was assumed that the military responsibilities of our great self-governing colonies were limited to local defence and that the entire burden of furnishing reinforcements to any portion of the Empire against which a hostile attack in force might be directed must fall on the regular army. There may possibly have been some pious hope that in time of need the colonies might rally to the Mother Country, but no definite arrangements were made, nor were inquiries even on foot as to whether such aid might be expected, and if so, in what strength. Indeed, the necessity for it was by no means realized, and its reliability was doubted.
You will remember that at that time Mr. Chamberlain was making a desperate effort to commit Canada to take part in the wars of the Empire. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier), then representing Canada, was strong in his stand that the delegates of Canada would not commit Canada to any policy wherein the troops of Canada would be called overseas, until first the people of Canada had pronounced upon it. To such proposals the Canadian delegates answered as follows:-
The Canadian Ministers regret that they have been unable to assent to the suggestion made by Lord Selborne respecting the navy, and by Mr St. John Broderick respecting the army. The Ministers desire to point out that their objections arise, not so much from the expense involved,- as from a belief that the acceptance of the proposals would entail an important departure from the principle of colonial selfgovernment
So strong was that opinion in the mind of my right hon. friend the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) that he made the statement in this House, not that the Militia Act of 1868, or the subsequent Militia Acts, including the most recent amendments, would be put in force, but that no law of conscription would be introduced, thereby acknowledging that conscription was not in force in this country. The right hon. leader of the Government said that the first line of defence is in France and in Flanders. Theoretically and for all intents and purposes he may be right, but will he still contend that the putting of the principle of conscription into force, whether the Act is constitutional, or whether it is not, does not constitute a radical change in the national life of this country? I do not think so. I hardly think that the Prime Minister will go that far. He says that the first line of defence is in France and Flanders. Tqeo-retically, I say again, he may be correct. He says, further, that Canada is defending herself and the Empire. I cannot follow him in that reasoning. Great Britain is defending France and Belgium; Canada and the other Dominions are aiding. So far I cannot admit that the Empire is on the defensive; I believe that we are still attacking. I cannot believe that our soldiers are called out to defend Canada. I take it that they are still voluntarily departing from our shores, imbued by the highest motives which can stir the hem, to defend Belgian neutrality and the rights of smaller nations to live a free life, fighting for the highest ideals of freedom and liberty. Will any man tell me, even my friend the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who was so stirred after reading in the bulletin the other day that some bombs had fallen over England, will even he tell me that Great Britain is now on the defensive? The right hon. gentleman says so, but I have yet to hear any statesman in the Empire other than he make, the statement that the Empire is now on the defensive. I cannot believe even the Prime Minister, when, standing >alone in this House, he dares to make such a state-

ment. But I can tell you that I do believe that the moment that Canada is ini danger and the moment Canada is on her defence, then it will not be a matter of getting 500,000 men to rush to the colours, but every man, young and old, in this country will take up arms.
I object to conscription, Sir, because I am opposed to the principle of coercion.
I am not a believer in coercive measures. The whole history of our country has been against coercion. Confederation was formed by the free will of the provinces to enter into a union. At the time of Confederation, whilst we had the might we did not consider that we had the right to coerce any other province of this Dominion into the union. Whenever any question arose as to coercing any section of the community or any province of the Dominion, immediately men in this House, upon both sides, stood up and said: hands off that section, or hand's off that province. Coercion has proved a failure wherever it has been adopted, whether in Poland, in Prussia or in Ireland. Prussian militarism is the worst form of coercion. Our men are to-day fighting Prussian militarism-and yet there are hon. gentlemen in this House who are trying to establish it here. If, on the other hand, we are not going out from our shores to prove our attachment to British institutions, then I say that every Dominion sharing equally in Empire benefits must share equally in Empire obligations. Canada must not bear more than Australia, nor Australia more than New Zealand or India, in proportion to population and respective advantages.
My next reason for being opposed to conscription is that there are no military reasons given by the right hon. Prime Minister, nor by any member of this House who advocates the measure, why conscription should be enforced in this country. When the war broke out, all the Government was willing to do was to secure the financial" and the industrial institutions of this country. All the Government seemed to be concerned with was to secure the manufacture of munitions in this country, and divide up the orders among their friends. The enormous war profits were to remain, and have remained, for the privileged few, and the Government, even to this day, has not the courage to say that they will conscript the wealth of this country and the industries of this country, but they are quite ready to say they will conscript the blood of the young men of this country. Patriotic [Mr. Bevlin.l
citizens came forward, and did a great deal at the beginning of the war. They offered large amounts towards defraying the expenses of the young men who were eager to go to the fighting lines. Let me say, also, that I want to give credit to hon. gentlemen upon the opposite side of the, House, as well as to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, for what they have generously done, in aiding the Allies and aiding this country. I wish to refer, for instance, to the gallant member representing Ste. Antoine Division, Montreal (Sir Herbert Ames). I am witness to the efforts which he has made towards raising money in order to benefit the families of soldiers who have gone to the front. I think, Sir, credit should be given to such men as the hon. member for St. Antoine, for the noble efforts they have inaugurated, to the mothers and fathers of this country, who allowed their sons to go out, in the first place, and to the sons, who nobly went out to fight for what they believed to be the highest principles of freedom and civilization. But I fail to see in what way the Government can claim any benefit for any action they have taken. What have the Government done? They have squandered the people's money. They paid out the money of this country. It was not their money, but the money of the people. It wtas the taxes paid by the people of this country. In regard to that, without wishing to enter into any recriminations whatever, I must say that most extravagant uses were made of that money, and we have had several years of war scandals. What the Government did, however, was this: they fixed the number of those who might go, but they made no provision for the families of the men who went, or for the men who might return. When the storms of indignation arose in certain parts of the country, a half-hearted action was taken, in the way of pensions. So many men agreed to go from every province of Canada, but, according to the Minister of Militia, the Prime Minister instructed him to go slowly in recruiting. The time having come to meet the ultra imperial clamour in the country, the Prime Minister made up his mind, and made the statement upon his own authority, not upon the authority of this House, nor upon the authority of Council, that 500,000 men should go. He did not give any military reason for that. He did not supply this House with any information. He simply said that 500,000 men would go. Now he says that he cannot get this 500,000 men, and the only way to obtain them is to con-

script those who remain, in order to make up the 500,000. I should like to know, Sir, before I cast a vote in favour of conscription, have the Imperial authorities asked us for more men? I see by the papers that General Currie, the general commanding the Canadian forces abroad, has said he requires more officers and more men. A statement was laid on the table of the House a few days ago, by the Government, to the effect that there were thousands of officers in England at the present moment. We know that officers are being returned to Canada, and the reason given is that there is no work for them to do. Does the Government wish to assume that, as General Gurrie said more officers and men are required, and that we must send more men and officers, or that we are simply to send the men. We have not that information, Sir, and in order to make up our minds just how we should vote, it is necessary that we should have it. Does England ask for reinforcements? We are told that there are 2,000,000 men in the way of reinforcements, in England. Further the statement is made that there are some 3,500,000 m England at the present moment of military age, who have escaped conscription. We are told further, since we must rely upon statements for our information in making up our minds upon this question, that there are in England, at the present moment 1,200,000 men who are occupied at works which are entirely useless in connection with the war, engaged in hotels, brokers' offices and theatres. I wonder if the hon. gentleman from Ked Deer thought of those 1,200,000 men when he turned to us upon this side of the House, and said: "Do you know that at this moment, according to the bulletin, bombs are falling over the city of London?" That is information which we should have, and no such information has been given to us. What was the attitude in the British House of Commons when information was asked? It is to be found in the words of Sir Edward Grey, when he was advising the House of Commons what attitude should be taken. Here is what he said:
The most awful responsibility is resting upon the Government in deciding what to advise the House of Commons to do. We have disclosed our mind to the House of Commons. We have disclosed the issue and the information which we have.
I ask hon. gentlemen, in all fairness to the members of this Hou^e, who have given this matter just as serious consideration as they have, in all fairness to the men
throughout the provinces of this Dominion, have they given us reasonable information upon which we can base a judgment, or upon which they may base a judgment? Will the right hon. gentleman tell us that he has not that information? What does he say in this House? On June 15, 1917, in repeating the words of the Prime Minister of England; he said:
The British Cabinet became for the time being an Imperial War Cabinet. While It was in session, its overseas members had access to all the information which was at the disposal of His Majesty's Government, and occupied a status of absolute equality with that of the members of the British War Cabinet. It had prolonged discussions on all the most vital aspects of Imperial policy, and came to important decisions in regard to them-decisions which will enable us to prosecute the war with increased unity and vigour, and which will he of the greatest value when it comes to the nego tiations of peace.
I wanted to find out, before making up my mind on the subject, what information the , Prime Minister had that he might give to this House. I asked him this question:
Mr. Devlin:	Was there any discussion as to
what would be the best form to be adopted in prosecuting the war for a concerted action on the part of the different dominions beyond the seas?
After which the discussion proceeded:
Sir Robert Borden:	The institution of the
Imperial Cabinet itself was entered upon with the view that the consultation thus brought about would result in greater unity of purpose and in more effective co-operation.
Mr. Devlin: .Was any decision reached by the members of that committee or Cabinet as to what concerted action should he taken by the Dominions beyond the seas?
Sir Robert Borden:	No special consideration
was given to any matter of that kind. The deliberations were of a general character with regard to the conduct of the war and the task that had to he accomplished, and the best means of fulfilling that task.
And, Sir, the Prime Minister says that this measure is the result of his own judgment, not of anything that he heard during his attendance at the Imperial War Cabinet or from the Imperial authorities. He did not even question the Imperial authorities; he said that he would resent any questioning of the Imperial authorities on a matter of that kind. But when the naval proposals were before this House the Prime Minister did not hesitate to ask the Im- . perial authorities for advice. He then said that he had sought and obtained information from the Admiralty Department, which information was in the form of a memorandum; and wanted to commit the members of this House and the people of Canada to that memorandum, which was dictated by a gentleman who has since been

people and for the people of Canada. As a Canadian I want to say that the moment you attempt to legislate against the will of a great section of the people without giving them a chance to pronounce upon the measures proposed, you are legislating in spite of the rights of the people, and are infringing upon that constitution which has always been the guarantee of Canadian liberty and Canadian security. You are disrupting the work of Confederation, and that on the eve of the fiftieth anniversary of Confederation. You are throwing our province into the turmoil of strife, thereby defeating the very aim which we all have in view, the aiding of our Allies and standing by the boys in the trenches. No Government in this country, no Parliament, no political party, has a monopoly of patriotism, but all are imbued with the strongest possible love of country. You want to stand by the boys in the trenches? So do we. Those boys are as dear to us as they are to any hon. gentleman seated opposite. We will stand by them, and we will stand by them with hon. gentlemen opposite; but we must at least he allowed to say that in our judgment and in our conscience the measure taken by this Government will not have the effect of standing by the boys in the trenches.
Coercive measures are unnecessary, and they will be resented. Economy in your expenditure; the organization of your efforts to develop trade and industry; the encouragement of agriculture; increased production, are the urgent needs of to-day-to-morrow will bring other and new problems. Mr. Speaker, I have heard since my childhood that "Britons never shall be slaves." I say that Canadians never shall be slaves to an autocratic and irresponsible Government. A*nd any Government which to-day, in view of the opinions openly expressed in this country, and knowing the temper of the Canadian people who may be for, or who may be against, the measure now proposed, attempts to enact it without the free will of the people being heard, is both autocratic and irresponsible.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when a member
of Parliament is called upon to decide his course of action, there are two conceptions of duty which have to be reckoned with. On the one hand, he may regard himself as the mouthpiece of his constituency; he may consider that he is here to record what he believes to be the will of the majority

of those who sent him. On the other hand, occasions sometimes arise where he is in possession of fuller information, and has greater opportunities for consideration of a question than his constituents, and where the duty rests upon him to follow his conscience and to lead rather than follow those whom he represents. Most of us have been elected in this House as exponents of certain fixed principles. When a question arises that affects those principles, our course is easy, our constituents know what to expect of us, and we do what they ex-unforeeeen and unexpected, we aTe thrown upon our own resources. We then are compelled to take stock of the situation; to arrive at decisions; to take a position; and we must be ready to stand or fall by that decision when the time comes for us to again meet those who sent us. Fortunate indeed is the member of the House whose personal inclinations, the known views of whose constituents, and the tenets of whose party all coincide. He has only to swim down the current; everything is going his way. He has very little occasion for selfglorification, lese occasion for criticism of others whose position is difficult, and no occasion whatever to condemn the conscientious action of his fellow-members.
Since this measure was introduced in the House, I have received a number of communications from my constituents. These have come in the form of petitions, of resolutions, of personal letters. They are on both sides of the question; some are for and some are against the Bill. An organization in Montreal known as "La Ligue Patriotique des interete Canadiens," sent me a number of petitions signed extensively by people I know. Many of these are citizens of standing in my constituency; many of them are the wives and mothers of persons well known in my bity. That is an example of what ie coming on one side. On the other hand, I have received a resolution of the Board of Trade, the President of which is a French-Canadian, in favour of conscription. I have received 9 p.m. resolutions from various church organizations. And I have received two resolutions, one from the English and one from the French branch of the Great War Veterans of the Province of Quebec. Among the petitions I have received the one which in some respects is the most notable is that which comes from the French section of the Great War Veterans of the city of Montreal. I know the men who make up that organization. Many

of them have served at the front with honour to themselves and to their race. The president, the vice-president, the secretary and the treasurer were all members of that famous 22nd Battalion which again and again has had its ranks filled up, and which has covered itself with glory, as we all so well know. These men, I think, can speak with some authority. They have been overseas; their motives cannot be impugned; they have themselves seen conditions at the front; they know the needs and the wastage; they have left their comrades still fighting; they have seen what it means *when the Hun retreats from devastated France; they have every reason to know, to know to the full, what it would mean if we should lose this war. A resolution passed unanimously by a body of that kind is a resolution which I must certainly receive with respect. Let me read it to you. It is in French, but I think we shall all understand it just the same:-
Association Canadienne des Veterans de la Grande Guerre, section frangaise.
Propose par J. C. Poirier, appuyd par E. Frereault.
Consid6rant que 1'enrSlement volontaire non-seulement dans Quebec mais le Dominion en-tier est devenu pratiquement chose du passe. Considdrant que pour seconder les efforts des Allies et mener Cette guerre & bonne fin, de nouvelles troupes sont immddiatement requises. Considerant que le Gouvernement a le pouyoir de mettre en force l'Acte de la milice.
Qu'il soit rdsolu :-
Que la section' frangaise de Montreal, bran-che de l'Association des Veterans de la Grande Guerre demanae au Gouvernement d'imposer le service obligatoire pour tout homme valide de 20 a 45 ans de maniere a ce:-
Riches comme pauvres Professionnels comme ouvriers Patrons comme employes Maries conrme ceiibataires Etrangers comme citoyens puissent faire leur part pour la cause commune des Allies, (Adopte a l'unanimite.)
Mr. O'. A. WILSON: Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell us by whom that is signed, or if it is signed at all?^

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
I will be glad to translate it into English or to read the English version as published in the papers. I shall read the whole extract:
At a meeting of the French section of the War Veterans' Association (L'Association Canadienne des Soldats de Retour du Front), held this morning in the rooms of the association, 20 La Presse Building, the following resolution, which will be sent forthwith to the Prime Minister of Canada , was adopted unanimously:
"Proposed by J. C. Poirier, vice-president of the association, seconded by E. Frerault, secretary :
"Considering that voluntary enlistment has practically ceased, not only in the province of Quebec but in the whole Dominion generally;
"Considering that the Government has the power to put the Militia Act into force,, be it resolved:
"That the French Section of the District of the War Veterans' Association request that compulsory service be imposed on all available men in Canada between the ages of 20 and 45.
They go farther than we do.

It is as follows:
In my humble opinion the defence of Canada implies not only the power to safeguard the territory itself and the lives and property of Canadians, it further includes the faculty recognized in international law to prevent, by all legitimate means, the invasion, ruin and sacking of the country, in attacking the enemy in his own country, pursuing him everywhere, destroying his resources, giving him no rest until he be reduced to utter powerlessness. The very legitimate necessity of opposing an onslaught quite naturally justifies the attack of the enemy in his own country or wherever he may seek refuge. It often is by taking the offensive, attacking and invading, that the defence of one's own country may be better attended to. It would indeed be imprudent, if not utterly reckless, for a country at war, to be content with a defensive strategy and to refrain from hostilities until the country were invaded and sacked.
I am sure that no one in this House or out of it will venture to suggest that the Chief Justice of Quebec, the Hon. Sir Francois Lemieux, is not an authority on matters of that kind, that he does not speak as a man who knows what he is speaking about. Every one will agree that he speaks as one who has studied deeply constitutional questions and is well qualified to give an opinion thereon. In his opinion, the best war of defence is a war of attack, wherever the enemy may be.
A good deal of time has been spent in this House in explaining the origin of the Militia Act of 1904, and going back and citing many of the opinions held at the time of the enactment of the original Militia Act and its various amendments There seems to me no real ground for contendng that even under the Act of 1904 conscription is not permissible. I think we all admit that the Act of 1904, under certain circumstances, contemplates wholesale conscription. The only difference of opinion is as to whether, under the old Militia Act, that conscription should be for men who could be sent, against their will, overseas. I do not pretend to discuss that point. I understand that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who was at the time Minister of Justice and Who is now Chief Justice of Canada, was of opinion, when that Act was passed, that it did permit men to be sent overseas. I understand that that is the opinion of the law officers of the Crown to-day. Not being a lawyer, I am willing to accept that opinion, considering my own in that respect to be of no great value. But I do not think that is the vital question. In any event the principal question with us is, how can we do what we want to do? And if the law already on the statute books is not sufficient, the quickest and simplest course is to pass an Act that will be sufficient, and if I rightly read the Bill that is now before the House, section 2 covers the situation as fully as an Act can.
Every male British subject who comes within one of the classes .... shall be liable to be called out as hereinafter provided on active service in the Canadian Expeditionary Force for the defence of Canada, either in or beyond Canada,-
-unless he falls under certain exemptions. We will all admit, I think, that this Act will meet the circumstances of the case, and if the old Act leaves any doubt, the sooner we can pass an Act in which the purpose, the destination and the method is clear, I think the better it will be for our country and its defence.
I have listened attentively to many of the speeches made in this House since this Bill was introduced. There is very little new that can now be said. We all admit that it only remains for us individually, so to speak, to make our confessions and to endeavour to clarify the situation in our own minds and those of our constituents. But certain objections have been raised, and those objections have been put forth

with logic, with reason and with sincerity-? I for my part feel that some of the objections should be answered, or that at least an attempt should be made to answer them.
The first objection that has been advanced is that the need for men is not so apparent as to justify this measure. The other night the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley), who sits on the opposite side of the House, attempted to show that there were
126.000	reserves in England and 90,000 here. His figures fell down completely when they were analyzed, but it is "well that the actual figures should be placed on Hansard in concrete form. It is true that there are
126.000	men in England, but only one-half of those are combatants, 30,000 of them are ready for the firing line, 35,000 more will be fit in the course of the next few months;
65.000	all told will be the sum total of combatant reinforcements out of that. 126,000 men. In Canada to-day there are less than
20.000	who may be regarded as in class A, that is men who will eventually be fit for the trenches. But the most significant figures of all are those in respect to infantry recruiting. We are told that the infantry losses are generally the greatest at the front. In April and May our casualties amounted to 23,939. These were largely infantry, and you will see that this involves a wastage of over 10,000 men a month.
How many men have we been recruiting throughout Canada during the last five months to make up the wastage in infantry? In January 5,707, in February there were 2,358; in March, 2,286; in April, 1,794; in May, 1,208 or an average of 2,670 infantrymen recruited in Canada since the year began. It needs no abstruse calculation in arithmetic to demonstrate that, if our casualties are 10,000 a month, and our infantry reinforcements not more than a quarter of that number, the thne is not far distant when the infantry reinforcements on hand will be exhausted, unless some steps are taken to secure more men. It is true there were 34,376 enlistments in the first five months of this year, but a very large proportion of those is composed of non-combatants. They were 13,353 infantry, 4,187 artillerymen, 8,317 forestry and railroad construction battalions, 8,523 miscellaneous arms of the service. Not more than one half of the total number, therefore, may be considered as infantry and artillery, which are the real combatant forces. It takes from eight to twelve months to train men for the firing line, and, even if we should now raise the men authorized under the Bill, if

it- passes, it would be 1918, probably, before the first of them would be used for service in France. It, therefore, does not admit of delay, because the reserve that we have on hand will be exhausted by Christmas, and after Christmas, what are we to do for more men?
There is no man who is to-day better qualified to speak of the military situation than the commander in chief of our forces in France. Even at the risk of repeating what may have been said by others, I want to read the recent messages from General Sir Arthur Currie, who knows more about the military situation overseas than any other living man. When he received a telegram of congratulation upon his recent honour, from the Prime Minister of Canada, his reply contained this significant clause:
It is an imperative and urgent necessity that steps be immediately taken to insure that sufficient drafts of officers and men are sent from Canada to keep the corps at its full strength.
And immediately after being interviewed by Mr. F. A. Mackenzie of the Montreal Star, General Currie said:
"I've no wish to interfere with current political controversies, but my personal conviction is that the only solution to the problem of Canadian recruiting is conscription. I believe that many difficulties which now threaten the adoption of such a policy would disappear before prompt and bold action.
"My experiences in France have shown me, not as a politician, but as a soldier, the necessity of conscription, if we desire to maintain at full strength our fighting divisions to the end."

There are none of U3 probably who have not friends overseas, probably none of us who have not relations and intimate friends in the firing line, and I ask those who are in receipt of letters from those boys overseas from week to week, what do the boys ask for? Do they not write and say: " Send us reinforcements; we need them more than anything else?" One of the bravest men I ever knew, and one of my personal friends, Colonel Victor Buchanan, killed not long ago, served in a Montreal Highland regiment. The last letter he wrote me had one note in it from end to end: " We need men; our Highland regiment is being filled up with drafts from every part of Canada; do tell the people of Montreal to send us more Montreal Highlanders, so that our ranks may be filled." Can any man with a sympathetic heart turn a deaf ear to letters from those he has known all his life, when they ask that they be not abandoned on the firing line?
Another objection which is raised is that this Parliament is incompetent to pass such an Act. It is said that Parliament is six years old, that there are twenty vacancies, and that a number of additional constituencies, under the new distribution, are entitled to members. That is an absolutely erroneous idea. No question can be raised, by any one who knows anything about legal or constitutional law, 'as to our right to pass such a measure as this. Our constitution is the British. North America Act and its amendments. The amendments are just as valid as the Act. If the Act tells us that the life of Parliament is five years, and the amendment extends it to six, seven, ten, or twenty, the amendment is just as valid as the original Act, and any Act we may pass in this Parliament, while it is legally constituted, is equally valid, whether it be passed in the first or the last year of our incumbency in office. The question whether we have a moral right is another matter, but the legal right is absolutely in-eontestible. My hon. friend, the member
for St. Mary's, the mayor of Montreal (Mr. Martin) asked me a question a moment ago as to whether we could spare the men. In his judgment, as first magistrate of the city of Montreal, he believed we could not. I would like to discuss that with him for a moment, because we are both interested alike in that great city. I have noticed in this-Parliament that the hon. gentlemen who ask us to give the voluntary system another - trial are the very ones who say we eannot spare the men. If we cannot spare the men raised by conscription, how can we spare them when they are raised by the voluntary system? In fact, the men that might be raised by a continuation of the voluntary system would be far lees easily spared than the men that will be obtained by conscription.
